schools.summary: Matthew Henry reads the opposition as the old enmity of the serpent against God's temple, and finds the second house's glory the greater for being built amid it; the builders are 'children of the captivity,' the foes a mongrel people who said they were Jews and were not.
Ellicott identifies the adversaries as the mixed Samaritan race whose Israelite element was lost among tribes imported by Sargon, Sennacherib, and Esar-haddon (2 Kings 17:24-34).
Wesley and Clarke agree: the relics of the ten tribes and the foreign nations Assyria's kings settled in the land.
Gill names them simply the Samaritans.

Ellicott reads 'we seek your God as ye do' against 2 Kings 17:33 (they feared the Lord and served their own gods) — hypocrites or syncretists, counted enemies; the appeal to Esar-haddon (d. c. 668 B.C.) speaks from a century-and-a-half tradition.
Wesley: the offer was insincere, a bid to pry into the Jews' counsels for matter of accusation; they sought God in a mongrel way (2 Kings 17:26). Clarke: fair words, but no friendly intention.
Gill notes they addressed the principal men, Zerubbabel and the chief of the fathers, knowing all turned on winning them.

Keil hears in 'our God' and 'Jahve the God of Israel' a pointed rebuttal of the Samaritan claim, 'we together' meaning we alone. Ellicott defends the refusal as in harmony with God's will (cf. 2 Kings 17), not intolerance — a single concession would have defeated the whole Restoration.
Clarke: they could not own the Samaritans as true worshippers. Wesley: another nation and religion, outside Cyrus's grant — trust God with confidence but men with caution.
Gill: prince, high priest, and chief of the people answered with one voice.

Keil identifies 'the people of the land' with the adversaries of v.1, reads the participle as continued harassment, glosses 'weaken the hands' (cf. Jer. 38:4), and notes the marginal reading 'terrify/alarm' (2 Chron. 32:18).
Gill lists the tactics: threats, dissuading workmen, cutting off materials from Tyre and Sidon (Ezra 3:7) and money from the royal revenues.
Clarke: discouraged and opposed the work by every possible means.

Keil leaves the means open (bribed ministers or retained agents) but dates the stoppage from the second year of the return through Cyrus's remaining reign (cf. Dan. 10:2); Ellicott traces the eight years of paid agents through Cambyses and the pseudo-Smerdis to Darius son of Hystaspes.

Clarke: corrupted court officers stalled Cyrus's orders; the Darius is Hystaspes' son. Wesley: Cyrus favoured the Jews but was diverted by war, leaving the hostile Cambyses as viceroy; 'until Darius' spans Cyrus, Cambyses, and the magician.
Gill: the hired men worked to withhold the money or to get Cyrus's edict revoked.

Keil makes the identity of Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes the hinge of the whole section, to be settled from the letter's contents; the rare word for 'accusation' (from a root 'to bear enmity') betrays its purpose. Ellicott: Ahasuerus is Cambyses, who reigned ~7 years and let the work languish.
Henry: with Cyrus's protection gone, the church's watchful enemies struck at once; the letter is an 'accusation,' the devil (accuser of the brethren, Rev. 12:10) working through human instruments.
Clarke and Wesley agree Ahasuerus is Cambyses, son of Cyrus, no friend to the Jews.
Gill reports Jarchi's minority guess (Esther's husband) but sides with the majority (Josephus): Cambyses.

Ellicott: the Artaxerxes is Gomates the Magian who personated Smerdis (7 months), marked by 'in the days of' vs. 'in the reign of'; he weighs and rejects the Longimanus/Xerxes scheme on the strict sequence and the linking word 'ceased.' Keil: the identity is the hinge, to be read from the letter; Rehum = royal counsellor, Shimshai = secretary.
Clarke identifies the Magian usurper (Oropaestus/Smerdis/Mardus/Sphendatates) feigning Cambyses' brother; Wesley keeps Cambyses under his Persian name.
Gill takes Artaxerxes for Cambyses, rejecting the short-reigned Smerdis as an unlikely correspondent.

debates.question: Who is the Artaxerxes of Ezra 4:7?

sides.position: the Magian usurper (pseudo-Smerdis / Gomates) who reigned only seven months

schools.summary: Clarke notes the Aramaic portion begins here (through Ezra 6:18) and argues the verbatim preservation of the documents, in their own tongue and character, is a mark of the historian's scrupulous authenticity.
Ellicott fixes the titles: Rehum the chancellor is the 'lord of judgment,' the civil governor's style; Shimshai the scribe the royal secretary.
Gill reports Jarchi's account of the drafting (Rehum composing, Shimshai writing) but judges it sent in all their names.

Keil notes the clumsy anacoluthon (a catalogue of senders where the letter should begin) heaped up 'to give weight'; Ellicott traces the peoples — Persians, Babylonians of Cuthah and Ava (2 Kings 17:24), Susians, Median Pharathiakites, men of Erech (Gen. 10:10) — the Dinaites and Tarpelites only conjecturally.
Gill takes them for the governors of the several nations, all subscribing the letter.
Clarke leaves Asnappar unidentified (Shalmaneser? Esar-haddon? his escorting officer?); Wesley leans to Esar-haddon or an eminent captain of the colony.

Ellicott: Asnappar cannot be Esar-haddon but was probably his chief officer; 'and at such a time' = 'and so forth.' Keil guards against inferring the Jews were transported by Artaxerxes — 'came up from thee' means from beyond the Euphrates.
Gill takes 'brought over' of the river Euphrates.

debates.question: Who was Asnappar who resettled the colonists?

sides.position: Esar-haddon himself or another eminent king / escorting captain
not Esar-haddon, but probably his chief officer

schools.summary: Clarke surveys the long perplexity over 'and at such a time' — Vulgate, the early English Bibles (Coverdale, Becke, Barker), and Calmet's emendation 'and at this time,' a courteous wish of health.
Ellicott renders 'on this side the river' as beyond the Euphrates (the court's standpoint) and 'and at such a time' as 'and so forth' — a courtly formula, not a clue.
Gill: a genuine copy Ezra brought from Babylon, its text in the five following verses.
Henry exposes the falsehood: the Jews had only begun the temple, no walls being built or designed (as Neh. 1:3 shows the ruins long after) — 'false tongues, false pens,' sharp arrows (Ps. 120:3-4).

Ellicott finds virulence and exaggeration in every line, though the charge here is only 'preparing walls' (sharpened in vv.13, 16); Keil: 'came up from thee' means from beyond Euphrates, not that the king sent them.
Wesley: a mere fiction, confidently affirmed to be believed by a king whose ears the accusers already possessed.
Gill: the letter's whole point was to make the king believe Jerusalem was rising again.
Keil and Ellicott parse the three imposts (measured tax/tribute, consumption duty, road toll; cf. Ezra 7:24) and correct the close to 'at length damage will be done to the kings.'
Henry: groundless prognostication — that Jerusalem would refuse tribute and draw the whole trans-river country into revolt; every line breathes the serpent's malice.
Clarke divides the taxes differently (capitation, excise, land tax) and paraphrases: fortify the city and they will pay you nothing.
Gill: the king is pressed to weigh it seriously with his counsellors.

Keil: 'to salt salt' = to eat salt = to be in the king's pay, setting aside the rabbinic/Lutheran reading 'we who destroyed the temple' (salt on ruins, Judg. 9:45); Ellicott: a general figure of dependence on the king.
Clarke: salt is the emblem of an incorruptible covenant, those who ate it bound to fidelity — but these were hypocrites in the Persian pay.
Henry: enmity to the gospel gilded with pretended loyalty to Caesar; yet the figure rebukes believers, who are 'salted with God's salt' and should resent his dishonour.
Gill: salaried posts under the king, honour anciently paid in salt (Pliny's salaria).

Keil: the 'book of records' is the royal chronicle (cf. Esther 6:1), 'thy fathers' the king's predecessors in government back to Chaldean and Assyrian kings. Ellicott: 'of old time' = 'from the days of eternity'; exaggeration, if not falsehood, in every word.
Gill takes the records for those of the Babylonian monarchy, with the Medes and Persians joined.
Clarke: the records of the Chaldeans, to whom the Persians succeeded.

Keil reads the verse as the climax of the indictment — a fortified Jerusalem costing the king his supremacy west of Euphrates; Ellicott calls it the same unscrupulous language, disproportionate to a remnant that could scarcely build a temple, though perhaps hinting at general disaffection.
Gill notes the claim that the city was rebuilt 'as it formerly was' and now again attempted.

themes: empire said to be at stake
a defenceless community made a threat

schools.summary: Henry: the king suffered himself to be imposed upon, taking the charge for granted — the hard fate of princes who see with other men's eyes; against which stands God's judgment, always just because it sees things as they are.
Keil glosses the opening term as a decree (a Persian loanword), the 'peace, and so forth' a courtly formula; Ellicott notes address and reply are blended as before.
Gill: that the king answered at all honoured the adversaries and gave them the authority they sought.
Keil insists 'plainly' (a participle 'made plain,' used adverbially) means distinctly read aloud in open court, not 'translated into Persian,' and links it forward to the commanded search of v.19.
Gill notes the courtly plural 'unto us,' the settled royal style.

Keil renders the verb 'lifted itself up' rebelliously (cf. 1 Kings 1:5) and grants a basis — Jerusalem's revolts against Babylon; Ellicott insists the insurrection was never against Persia, only against the fallen Babylon (2 Kings 24) the Persians had supplanted.
Clarke: 'insurrection' is the victor's word — Israel's God-given struggles for independence are branded rebellion only because they failed, as 1688 is a 'Revolution' only because it succeeded.
Gill: the search was made in the records of the king's Chaldean or Persian predecessors.

outliers.note: Turns the verse into a reflection on political language: 'it is an easy thing to find a staff to beat a dog' — rebellion versus revolution is decided by who wins, illustrated by England's 1688.

themes: a true fact wrenched from context

schools.summary: Keil: the dominion west of Euphrates holds in full only of David and Solomon, faintly of later kings; Ellicott extends the line to a few kings down to Josiah, cited historically though outside Persian annals.
Clarke supplies the proof-texts: David's conquests (2 Sam. 8:3) and Solomon's rule from the river to the border of Egypt (1 Kings 4:21).
Gill names David and Solomon as the 'mighty kings.'

Henry marks the silence about the temple: neither letter nor decree mentions it, since both knew Cyrus's command to rebuild it stood unrepealed; the prohibition was confined to the city walls — a fault-line the next verses tear open.
Keil reads the closing clause as reserving to the king a future command to build — the work only stayed, not forbidden outright.
Clarke: the rebuilding was only provisionally suspended — 'let it cease for the present,' the door shut but not bolted.
Gill: the men are simply to be made to cease from building.
Keil renders 'be warned from committing an oversight' (a word for one put on his guard), the king's motive naked self-interest — the same fear of lost revenue planted in v.13.
Henry: the king would not that the crown should lose by his wearing it — moved by a tax never in danger, he lends his empire to a lie.
Gill: a charge to execute the order at once, though the report of wall-building was a great falsehood.

themes: a small motive, a great harm
the state turned against the church

schools.summary: Henry (with Wesley): as the accusers abused the king in obtaining the order, so in executing it — the decree touched only the walls, but they stretched the general clause 'cause these men to cease' to the temple, their real target; their feet ran to evil (Prov. 1:16).
Clarke: they forced the Jews to desist on pain of the king's displeasure, probably with an armed band; Wesley draws the lesson to pray for all in authority, not kings only.
Keil renders 'by violence and force' (arm/violence), rejecting Bertheau's 'with forces and a host' — raw compulsion, not an army.
Gill: the letter was read before those to whom it was directed, setting the swift reaction in motion.

themes: a decree stretched to the temple
malice supplies what the law withheld

schools.summary: Keil explains the architecture: v.24 resumes v.5 (delay until Darius) after the parenthesis of accusations, adding the precise 'second year'; warns against reading vv.23-24 as successive. Ellicott adds the suspension lasted nearly two years, but the altar remained a centre of worship.
Wesley names Darius son of Hystaspes; Clarke dates the work from Cyrus's first year (c. 536 B.C.) to the desisting (c. 522) and on to Darius's second year (c. 519).
Henry judges from the thread of the history that it was Darius Hystaspes.
Gill: we are not told how far the work had gone — perhaps just above the foundation — before it ceased.
